# Book Pages 1–556 # Constituted Text Only; Critical Apparatus Removed ## (Br. 1.21–30; Vi. I. 2.1–8)
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the supreme self, who is changeless, pure, eternal, whose form is always of one nature, and who is the conqueror of all living beings. || 1 ||
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara; to Vāsudeva, the Savior, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction! || 2 ||
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, who possesses both singular and manifold natures, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and who is both unmanifest and manifest. || 3 ||
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is himself composed of the world! || 4 ||
Having prostrated before the Imperishable, the Supreme Person, who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and who dwells within all beings; (5)
That which is by its very nature consciousness, utterly pure from the perspective of ultimate reality, appears as the nature of an object due to erroneous perception. || 6 ||
To Viṣṇu, the devourer of the universe, the Lord of its maintenance and creation, the omniscient Master of the worlds, unborn, undecaying, and immutable; || 7 ||

Having prostrated before the Lord of the Universe, who is primordial and most subtle, and before Brahmā and the others, as well as the one who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; || 8 ||
Having bowed down to my preceptor, the lordly son of Parāśara, who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, I shall proclaim this Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas.
I shall relate how, in the past, when questioned by Dakṣa and other most excellent sages,
the blessed Grandfather, born from the lotus, spoke.
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 4 | A.
I shall proclaim the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of supreme splendor;
listen as I recount it to you in detail and in proper sequence! || 1 ||
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods:
Sahasrada, Payoda, Kroṣṭā, Nīla, and Añjika. || 2 ||
The three heirs of Sahasradasyu were supremely righteous. || 3 ||
Haihaya, Haya, and likewise King Veṇuhaya;
the heir of Haihaya was known as Dharmanetra. || 4 ||
The son of Dharmanetra was Kārta, and his son was Sāhañja;
[there was a city named Sāhañjanī].
She was established as the queen by that king;
Kunti was the daughter of Dharmanetra, and Sahañja was his son.
The heir of Sāhañja was the king named Mahiṣmān. || 5 ||
[The city named Māhiṣmatī was founded by which king.
There was a powerful son of Mahiṣmata named Bhadraśreṇya.
Indeed, King Dhīpa of Vārāṇasī has already been mentioned previously. || 6 ||
The heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the king named Durmada;
the wise and heroic son of Durmada was named Kanaka. || 7 ||
The four heirs of Kanaka were world-renowned:
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, and likewise Kṛtavarmā. (8)
Kṛtaujas was the fourth; from him was born Kṛtavīrya, and from him Arjuna was born, a king who possessed a thousand arms and ruled over the seven continents. || 9 ||
[He alone conquered the earth with a chariot possessing the splendor of the sun; for he,
having performed austerities for ten thousand years...]
Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, the son of Atri, by performing austerities that were exceedingly difficult to practice.
To him, Datta granted four boons of great splendor;
first, he chose as his initial boon a thousand arms. || 11 ||
When one is contemplating unrighteousness, there must be a restraint by the virtuous;
having conquered the earth through righteousness, one must protect it likewise through righteousness alone. || 12 ||
Having conquered many battles and slain thousands of enemies, his death occurred while he was engaged in combat against a superior foe on the field of battle. || 13 ||
Thus, by this fierce method, he has conquered this entire earth with its seven continents, its ports, its oceans, and its cities. || 14 ||
Indeed, as that wise one fought, his thousand arms appeared like those of the Lord of Yoga through the power of yoga.
It manifests through illusion. || 15 ||
By that king, seven hundred sacrifices were indeed performed according to the prescribed rites across the seven continents.
The best of sages are heard [to have said this]. || 16 ||
All the sacrifices of that mighty-armed one were accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
all of them had sacrificial posts made of gold, and all of them had altars made of gold. || 17 ||
All [these worlds] are adorned by highly fortunate gods stationed in their celestial chariots, and they are eternally graced by gandharvas and apsaras. || 18 ||
At whose sacrifice the learned Gandharva Nārada, the son of Varīdāsa, sang this verse,
being struck with wonder by his greatness: || 19 ||
Surely the destiny of Kārtavīrya cannot be attained even through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning. || 20 ||
For he, equipped with shield, sword, and bow, and mounted on a chariot, wandered through the seven continents.
The yogi is beheld by men. || 21 ||
No property was lost, there was no grief, and no confusion, as the Great King protected his subjects with righteousness according to their status. || 22 ||
For eighty-five thousand years, that lord of men became a universal monarch (cakravartin), an emperor possessing all jewels. || 23 ||
He himself became the cowherd and he himself was the guardian of the field;
through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna, the rain-god Parjanya by means of his showers. || 24 ||
With his thousand arms, their skin hardened by the striking of bowstrings, he indeed shines like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays. || 25 ||
For that one of great splendor, having conquered the sons of Karkoṭaka among the Nāgas in the city of Māhiṣmatī, established them there among men. || 26 ||
Indeed, during the rainy season, that lotus-eyed one, as if playing, caused the current of the ocean to flow upstream, breaking it apart with his arms. || 27 ||

The Narmadā, garlanded with wreaths of foam, was plundered by him as he played; she, whose thousands of moving waves were like frowning brows, approached him in fear. (28) She, whose thousands of moving waves were like frowning brows, approached him in fear. (28)
With his thousand arms, he plunged into the great ocean and raised up those rivers,
including the Narmadā swollen by the rains, so that they overstepped their shores.
As the great ocean was being agitated by his thousand arms, the great asuras dwelling in the netherworld remained motionless, hidden out of fear. || 29 ||

It had its great waves pulverized and its large fish and crocodiles tossed about; it possessed a mass of foam driven by the wind and was difficult to endure due to the agitation of its whirlpools. (30)

Then the king set it in motion; the king caused agitation with his thousand arms. With his thousand arms he [stirred] the ocean, which had been hurled by the gods and asuras, and was surrounded by the gods and asuras.
Like Mount Mandara [churning] the Ocean of Milk; like the Ocean of Milk itself.
Terrified by the agitation of Mount Mandara and struck with fear at the production of the nectar, they suddenly flew up in alarm upon seeing the formidable and supreme king. || 32 ||
Those great serpents remained with their heads bowed and motionless, like groves of plantain trees at evening when stilled by the absence of wind. || 33 ||
Having bound his bow with its string and, by means of five arrows,
having forcibly bewildered the lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, along with his army,
he conquered him, brought him under his control, and bound him in Māhiṣmatī. || 34 ||
Having heard that Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, had been bound by Arjuna,
the King then went there and, propitiating Arjuna, released the descendant of Pulastya.
He was entreated by Pulastya. || 35 ||
That thousand of arms produced a sound like that of a cloud at the end of a Yuga,
or like a crashing thunderbolt. || 36 ||
Oh, how great was the prowess of the descendant of Bhṛgu in battle, that he severed a thousand arms in combat, like a golden grove of palm trees! || 37 ||
Once, when he was thirsty, he was begged for alms by the Fire-god;
that hero gave the seven continents as alms to Vibhāvasu. || 38 ||
The fire blazed forth in every direction, desiring to consume his cities, villages, cowherd settlements, and entire territories. || 39 ||
By the power of that high-souled lord of men, Kārtavīrya, he consumed both the mountains and the forests. || 40 ||
That Citrabhānu, together with the Haihaya, burned the empty and delightful hermitage of Varuṇa’s son, along with the sacrificial islands. || 41 ||
The son whom Varuṇa obtained in former times, the radiant and most excellent one named Vasiṣṭha—that sage was also known as Āpava. || 42 ||
Thereupon, the powerful Āpava, out of anger, cursed Arjuna:
"O Haihaya, because you did not spare this [tree], and because this forest of mine has been burnt down by you, O Haihaya, your forest shall become famous [as the 'burnt' one]. (43)
Therefore, another shall perform that difficult task for you which you have undertaken:
the long-armed one named Rāma, the son of Kuntī named Arjuna, and the powerful son of Jamadagni. And he shall not become king. || 44 ||

"O Arjuna, the ascetic Brāhmaṇa Rāma of the Bhṛgu lineage— the one of great heroism, the best among strikers, and the mighty one— will crush you with his strength and, having severed your thousand arms, will slay you. (45)
No property was ever lost to that subduer of enemies, as the king protected his subjects through his majesty and his righteousness. (45)
Therefore, his death shall indeed come from Rāma,
due to the curse of that great sage;
likewise, this was the boon chosen by the royal seer himself in the past.
He had a hundred sons, five among whom were great chariot-warriors.
Skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous,
and illustrious were Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭi, and indeed Kṛṣṇa himself.
And there was a great king of Avanti named Jayadhvaja,
the son of Kārtavīrya.
They are energetic and possessed of great strength. || 48 ||
Jayadhvaja’s son was the very powerful Tālajaṅgha;
he had a hundred sons who were known as the Tālajaṅghas. || 49 ||
Five clans of those high-souled Haihayas are renowned:
the Vītihotras, the Saṃjātas, the Bhojas, and likewise the Āvantyas.
The Taṇḍikeras, the Vikrāntas, and likewise the Tālajaṅghas, as well as the Bharatas and the Sujātas, have not been enumerated individually due to their great number. || 51 ||
And other Yādavas of meritorious deeds, beginning with Vṛṣa, [arose]; Vṛṣa was the sustainer of their lineage, and his son was Madhu. || 52 ||
Madhu had a hundred sons, but Vṛṣaṇa was the founder of his lineage;
from Vṛṣaṇa all are called Vṛṣṇis, while from Madhu they are known as Mādhavas. || 53 ||
They are called Yādavas by the name of Yadu, and they are also known as Haihayas.
There shall be no loss of wealth for him, and he shall recover what was lost—anyone here who recounts the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya. || 58 ||
In this very world he becomes wealthy, and his merit increases;
as much as he sacrifices and as much as he gives, so shall he be honored in heaven. || 581 ||
O best of the twice-born, these five lineages of the sons of Yayāti, who were heroes of the world, have been proclaimed; they indeed uphold the worlds. || 582 ||

Having heard about the five elements, O best of sages, as well as the five classes of beings, both stationary and moving, and the five types of creation, the king, who was skilled in the matters of dharma and worldly affairs, [acted accordingly].
He becomes the master and lord of his five sons, and he shall obtain five boons that are difficult to attain in this world. || 584 ||
O twice-born ones, through the retention and hearing of these five groups, one obtains longevity, fame, sons, sovereignty, and prosperity as well. (585)
## Section 4. Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 4. B.
The Sages said: For what reason was the forest of the high-souled Āpava burnt?
Tell us who ask you how Kārtavīrya, having displayed his prowess, [attained that state]. || 11 ||
We have heard that this royal sage was a protector of his subjects;
how is it that, being their protector, he burned down that penance grove? || 12 ||
Sūta said:
The Sun-god approached Kārtavīrya in the form of a brahmin, desiring food; he said, "I am the Sun-god, of this there is no doubt. || 13 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, by what would you be satisfied? Tell me, O Maker of Day; what kind of food shall I give? Having heard, I shall provide it! (14)
The Sun said:
"O best among those who give food, grant me all that is stationary;
by that alone may I be satisfied, for I am not satisfied by anything else, O King! (15)
The king said:
"O best of those who radiate heat, it is not possible for any human power to consume all that is stationary; I bow down to you alone. || 16 ||
The Sun said:
"I am pleased with you; I give you inexhaustible arrows that face every direction, which, when discharged, shall blaze forth, endowed as they are with my own splendor. || 17 ||
"Today, being permeated by my splendor, this stationary object shall wither away;
having become dry, I shall reduce it to ashes, and by that, O lord of men, I shall find satisfaction. || 18 ||
Sūta said: Then the Sun-god gave arrows to Arjuna;
having obtained them, he indeed consumed everything, both the stationary and the moving. || 19 ||
Then [he saw] hermitages, villages, cow-pens, and cities; delightful penance-groves, forests, and pleasure gardens. || 110 ||
In this manner he consumed the eastern quarter, and thereafter the entire southern one;
the earth, stripped of trees and devoid of grass, was burnt by the solar radiance. || 111 ||
At that very time,
however, the great seer Āpava had been dwelling in the water for ten thousand years.
When his vow was completed, the great ascetic of immense splendor rose up.
That great seer saw that the hermitage had been burnt by Arjuna;
out of anger, he cursed the royal sage, just as I have related to you. || 113 ||
Listen to the lineage of the royal seer Kroṣṭu, which possesses supreme prowess;
for by merely hearing of the lineage of Kroṣṭu— the sustainer of Yadu’s line, a performer of sacrifices, and a doer of meritorious deeds— one is liberated from all sins.
In whose lineage was born Viṣṇu, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
To Kroṣṭu was born a son, Vṛjinīvān, of great renown; they consider Svāhi, the best of those who offer oblations, to be the son of Vṛjinīvān. || 3 ||
Svāheha had a son, King Uṣadgu, the best among speakers;
desiring offspring, he [Uṣadgu] indeed begot an excellent son. || 4 ||
He performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
his son was Citraratha, who was endowed with meritorious deeds. || 5 ||
The son of Citraratha was the heroic Śāśabindu, a performer of sacrifices who gave away abundant sacrificial fees and maintained the highest conduct.
He followed the path of the royal seers; he was a universal monarch, a great being of great heroism and many offspring. || 6 ||
In this regard, there is this genealogical verse (anuvaṃśa-śloka) which was sung by the ancients:
"Of the hundred sons of Śaśabindu, there were likewise a hundred [successors]. (7)
Among those wise men who were worthy [of their lineage] and possessed great wealth and splendor, there were six principal sons of great strength, known by the name Pṛthu. || 8 ||
Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas,
Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthudharman, and Pṛthumjaya.
Pṛthukīrti, the broad-giving king Śaśabindu, was his son. || 9 ||
The kings were the Śaśabindus. || 9 ||
Those who know the Purāṇas declare that Antara was the son of Pārthaśravas;
Suyajña was the son of Antara, and he had a son named Suyajña.
Uśanas performed the sacrifice in its entirety;
Uśanas, that righteous soul, [performed] his own duty, O best of those who desire [dharma].
Having obtained this earth,
those most virtuous kings performed one hundred horse-sacrifices. || 11 ||
Śineyu had a son named Auśanā, who was a scorcher of his enemies. || 11 ||
Marutta was his son, the most excellent among royal sages;
Marutta obtained an eldest son, Kambalabarhiṣ.
Out of indignation, he practiced the extensive Dharma even after death;
they desire a hundredfold progeny.
It was heard from Kambalabarhis. || 12 ||
Rukmakavaca was the son of Śataprasava;
having previously slain armored warriors in battle, Rukmakavaca [attained his name].
With sharpened arrows, the archer attained supreme glory;
at the horse sacrifice, the king bestowed sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins. || 14 ||
From Rukmakavaca was born Parāvṛt, the slayer of enemy heroes;
and from Parāvṛt were born five sons of great prowess. || 15 ||
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari—the father established Parigha and Hari in Videha. || 16 ||
Rukmeṣu became king, and Pṛthurukma was his dependent;
Jyāmagha, having been expelled from the kingdom by those two, lived in a hermitage.
Though he was peaceful, dwelling in a hermitage, and had been exhorted by the Brahmins, he nevertheless took up his bow and, equipped with his banner and chariot, went to another region. || 18 ||
O King, having gone alone to the Narmadā, Mekalā, Mṛttikāvatī,
and the Ṛkṣavān mountain, he dwelt at Śuktimatī.
Jyāmagha’s wife was Śaibyā, a powerful and virtuous woman;
although that king was childless, he did not take another wife. || 20 ||
He was victorious in battle, and there he obtained a maiden;
that lord of men, being terrified, said to his wife, "She is my daughter-in-law. || 21 ||
Thus addressed, she said to him: "Whose daughter-in-law is this of yours?
Having heard that, Jyāmagha, the best of kings, replied:
"She shall be the wife of the son who will be born to you."

Through her fierce asceticism, she gave birth to that maiden; through the fierce asceticism of that maiden, Śaibyā was indeed brought forth. Having grown up, the fortunate Śaibyā gave birth to a son, Vidarbha. || 23 ||
Later, Vidarbha begot upon his daughter-in-law two wise princes, Kratha and Kaiśika,
who were heroes skilled in battle.
The third son was Lomapāda, who was supremely righteous. Babhru was the son of Lomapāda, and Dhṛti was his son. || 25 ||
Kaiśika’s son was Cidi; from him the kings known as the Caidyas descended. Bhīma was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his offspring. || 26 ||
From Kunti was born a son, Dhṛṣṭa, who was powerful and bold in battle.
To Dhṛṣṭa were born three heroic sons, all supremely righteous. || 27 ||
Āvanta, Daśārha, Balin, and Viṣahara;
the son of Daśārha was Vyoma, and the son of Vyoma is said to be Jīmūta. || 28 ||
Jimūtaputra was Vikṛti; his son was Bhīmaratha.
Now, it is said that Bhīmaratha had a son named Navaratha.
Constantly devoted to the duty of giving and dedicated to truth and virtue, his son was Navaratha; from him, Daśaratha is remembered. || 291 ||
His son was Daśaratha, and Śakuni was his son. From him came Karambha, and from him Kārambhī. From him came Karambhaka Dhanvī, who became King Devarāta. Thus Devarāta arose from him.
Devakṣatra became the king, the highly illustrious Daivarāti;
to Devakṣatra was born a son, equal to a divine embryo, who was named Nandana. || 31 ||
From Devakṣatra was born Devana, the delighter of the Kṣatriyas;
and from Devana was born Madhu.
From whom the arising of wisdom and wealth occurs. || 31 ||
King Madhu, the founder of the lineage of the Madhus and also sweet of speech,
was born from Madhu by the princess of Vidarbha.
The one who has many doors, the Supreme Person. || 32 ||
Madhu was of great splendor,
and from Madhu came Kuruvaśa; likewise, from Kuruvaśa a son was born.
The one who has many doors, the supreme among persons. || 32 ||
Then Aṃśu, the upholder of the Kuru lineage, was born to Bhadravatī, the princess of Vidarbha;
and Aikṣvākī became the wife of that Aṃśu, and from her he begot a son.
Endowed with all virtues, he increases the fame of the Sāttvatas among all beings. || 33 ||
Having understood this creation of the great-souled Jyāmagha,
one becomes joined with supreme joy and shall always possess progeny. || 34 ||
## Section 4. Genealogy | Chapter 4. C.
Kauśalyā gave birth to sons who were Sāttvatas, endowed with goodness:
Bhajina, Bhajamāna, Divya, and King Devāvṛdha. || 1 ||
And Andhaka, the great Bhoja, and Vṛṣṇi, the joy of the Yadus.
There are four lineages of these; hear them in detail: || 2 ||

Bhajamāna had two wives, Bāhyakā and Upabāhyakā, both of the Sṛñjaya lineage. From them, two daughters were born to Śṛñjaya, from whom many sons were produced. Of those, he married the two daughters of Bāhyakā.
Kṛmi, Kramaṇa, Dhṛṣṇu, Śūra, and Puraṃjaya—
these were born from Bhajamāna by Bāhyakāsṛñjayī. || 4 ||
Ayutājit, Sahasrājit, Śatājit, and Dāsaka were born from Bhajamāna by Upabāhyakā, the daughter of Sṛñjaya. || 5 ||
Among them, King Devāvṛdha performed supreme austerity, desiring:
"May I have a son endowed with all virtues. || 6 ||
Having thus composed himself, he touched the waters of the Parṇāśā; because of his constant ritual ablutions there, the river showed him affection. || 7 ||
Because of that king’s excellence, that best of rivers, overcome with anxiety, then went to Viñjughāṭaka, reflecting thus: || 8 ||
I do not find such a woman,
in whom there might be a son endowed with all these qualities for King Devāvṛdha.
Therefore, today both she and I have become united with him in our vows. || 9 ||
Then, having become a maiden and assuming a most excellent form, she chose the king as her husband, and that lord desired her. || 10 ||
In her, he of noble intellect conceived a radiant embryo;
then, in the ninth month, that best of rivers gave birth.
It is heard that those learned in the Purāṇas sing thus regarding this lineage: "From King Devāvṛdha was born Babhru, a son endowed with all virtues. (12)
Proclaiming the virtues of that high-souled Devāvṛdha, we see him from close at hand just as we hear of him from afar. || 13 ||
Babhru is the best among men; Devāvṛdha is equal to the gods.
Sixty-six are the men; fifty-six thousand are the men; and seventy-seven thousand are the men.
These have attained immortality, even from Babhru Devāvṛdha. || 14 ||
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, wise, devoted to the Brahmins, firm in his vows, illustrious, highly fortunate,
and a great chariot-warrior among the Sātvatas.
His lineage was very great; they were handsome and possessed of great splendor—the Bhojas of Mārttikāvata. From him [came] the Bhoja of Mṛttikāvatī. || 15 ||
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were the two wives of Vṛṣṇi.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends. || 16 ||
Mādrī [gave birth to] Yudhājit as her son, and then indeed Devamīḍhuṣa—
Anamitra, the conqueror of enemies, who was himself unconquered. || 17 ||
The son of Anamitra was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons: Prasena and Satrājit, both of whom were unconquered by enemy armies. || 18 ||
## Section 4. Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 5 | A.
Now, the god Mahādeva, formerly Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati—that lord of gods—for the sake of sport, [descended] among men for the sake of sport.
He was born even among humans. The Lord Nārāyaṇa was born.
Through the ascetic power of Vasudeva, the lotus-eyed one was born of Devakī with four arms, possessing a divine form and endowed with splendor. || 2 ||
The Lord, the Yogin Kṛṣṇa, who is light itself, has assumed human form;
he is the unmanifest Lord, the Master, appearing with manifest signs. || 2 ||
Nārāyaṇa, from whom proceeds both that which is perishable and that which is indeed imperishable—having become the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari was the eternal one. || 2 ||
He who in ancient times created Prajāpati from the lotus, that delighter of the Yādavas, having attained the state of being the son of Aditi. || 2 ||
The god known as Viṣṇu was born as the younger brother of Śakra;
it was he whom the Lord [Brahmā] propitiated for the sake of obtaining sons from Aditi.
For the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—
the Lord Nārāyaṇa took birth from the meritorious family of the wise Vasudeva, who was born in the lineage of Yayāti. || 2 ||
The oceans trembled, the mountains shook, and the sacred fires blazed forth at the birth of Janārdana. || 26 ||
Auspicious winds blew, the dust became stilled, and the celestial bodies shone with increased brilliance as Janārdana was being born. || 27 ||
The lunar mansion was named Abhijit, the night was named Jayantī, and the auspicious moment was named Vijaya, at which time Janārdana was born. || 28 ||
The unmanifest, eternal Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, was likewise born by means of his divine power (māyā), deluding all creatures. || 29 ||
And the Lord of the Thirty-three rained down a shower of flowers from the sky,
praising Madhusūdana with words full of auspiciousness.
The great seers, along with the Gandharvas, waited upon him by the thousands.
But Vasudeva [concealed] that son Adhokṣaja, who had been born during the night.
Having seen the god marked with the Śrīvatsa and endowed with divine characteristics, Vasudeva said to him: "O Lord, please withdraw this form! || 3 ||
"I am afraid of Kāṃsa, my dear, and therefore I speak thus: 'My sons, those elder brothers of yours of wondrous appearance, have been slain by him. || 4 ||
Having heard the words of Vasudeva, the Lord withdrew his form;
permitted by him, Pūtanā led him to the house of Nandagopa. || 5 ||
Abiding by the will of Ugrasena, he then gave [him] to Yaśodā. || 51 ||
At that same time, Yaśodā and Devakī were both pregnant;
Yaśodā was the wife of Nandagopa, that lord of Nandagopa. || 52 ||
On the very same night that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan, on that same night a daughter was born to Yaśodā. || 53 ||
But the highly illustrious Vasudeva, protecting her once she was born, gave a son to Yaśodā and took the daughter for himself. || 51 ||
Having given him to Nandagopa, he said, "Let him be protected;
this son of yours shall bring all prosperity to the Yādavas. (6)
But this child of Devakī shall remain in the world for as long as he slays Kaṃsa.
They are secure and bear the supreme burden. || 7 ||
But those kings who are wicked,
he will slay them all when the battle of the Kauravas has taken place.
In the assembly of all the kṣatriyas. || 71 ||
This god himself will act as Arjuna’s charioteer;
having rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas, he will depart.
He will consume what remains and shall lead the entire Yadu clan to the world of the gods. || 72 ||
For she is indeed like a daughter to you, and so she is to me; of this there is no doubt.
O mighty-armed one, do not strike her; let her go wherever she pleases. || 73 ||
That maiden grew up there in the residence of the Vṛṣṇis, being honored;
then the queen joyfully protected the goddess like her own son. || 74 ||
They say that she, born by this rite, was Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati;
indeed, she was born as the eleventh for the protection of Keśava. || 75 ||
And the Yādavas, with one-pointed minds, shall worship her;
for by her was Kṛṣṇa—the god of gods, possessed of a divine form—protected.
The sages said: For what reason did Kaṃsa, the Bhoja king of men, kill the young sons of Vasudeva? You ought to explain this to us! (77)
Sūta said:
Listen indeed, how Kaṃsa, being of vain intellect, crushed all those sons of Ānakadundubhi as they were born, one after another. || 78 ||
Just as Kṛṣṇa was born and exiled out of fear of the mighty-armed [Kamsa], and how Govinda, that Supreme Person, grew up among the cows. || 79 ||
It is said that at the wedding of the wise Vasudeva and Devakī, Kaṃsa, who was then the crown prince, served as the charioteer. || 710 ||
Then a divine voice from someone in the intermediate space spoke, exceedingly clear and a witness to the world: "Kaṃsa has been slain by Mātra. || 711 ||
"O Kaṃsa, that seventh embryo which you carry in your womb by means of this chariot for the sake of another—that shall be your death! || 712 ||
Hearing those words, the foolish Kaṃsa was then distressed;
drawing his sword, he then became intent on killing that girl. || 713 ||
The mighty-armed and powerful Vasudeva spoke to Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, out of friendship and affection: || 714 ||
No Kṣatriya whatsoever ought ever to kill a woman;
however, O delighter of the Yādavas, a means has been devised by me in this matter. (715)
O Lord of the Earth, whatever seventh embryo may be conceived in her, I shall bestow that upon you; therein you should act according to the proper sequence. || 716 ||
But you shall not now act according to your own will, O giver of many gifts;
for I shall bring even all your offspring under my control, Pṛthā included. || 717 ||
"O best of men, this speech shall not thus be false.
Having been addressed in this way and thus conciliated, he then accepted his daughters. || 718 ||
And Vasudeva, having obtained her as his wife, became joyful;
but the evil-doing Kaṃsa, of futile intellect, killed his sons. || 719 ||
The sages said:
"Who is this Vasudeva, and who is the illustrious Devakī?
Who is this Nanda the cowherd, and who is Yaśodā of great vows?"
Who gave birth to Viṣṇu, and who addressed him as "Tāṭa"? Who gave birth to his embryo, and who nurtured him? || 9 ||
Sūta said:
Kaśyapa was the Puruṣa, and Aditi is remembered as his beloved wife;
Kaśyapa was a portion (aṃśa) of Brahmā, and likewise Aditi was a portion of the Earth. || 10 ||
Nanda was proclaimed as Droṇa, and Yaśodā became Dharā.
Then the mighty-armed one fulfilled the desires of Devakī. || 11 ||
Those things which had been previously desired by that unborn Great Soul,
the divine one— whose self is yoga— having entered a human body, traversed the earth while deluding all beings through his yogic power (yogamāyā). || 12 ||
When dharma had perished, the Lord Viṣṇu was then born in the Vṛṣṇi clan to establish the order of dharma and to bring about the destruction of the asuras. || 13 ||
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and likewise Satyā Nāgnajitī,
as well as Subhāmā and Śaibyā.
Gāndhārī and Lakṣmaṇā likewise. || 14 ||
Mitravindā and Queen Kālindī, as well as Jāmbavatī,
Suśīlā, and Mādrī.
Kauśalyā and likewise Vijayā; || 15 ||
At that time, there were thousands of such goddesses as Vaidarbhī, Rukmiṇī, Kanyā, and Satyā, the daughter of Nagnajit.
Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Satrājit, as well as Jāmbavatī and Rohiṇī. || 14 ||
Śaibyā, Sudevī, Mādrī, another named Suśīlā,
Kālindī, and Mitravindā.
O Lakṣmaṇā, you who dwell within the net! || 15 ||
And sixteen. || 16 ||
As for those fourteen groups of Apsarases who were proclaimed in heaven, they have been selected by the gods and by Śakra, and have been sent here as the most distinguished. || 161 ||
Born in royal palaces for the sake of becoming the wives of Vāsudeva, these highly fortunate women are renowned as the consorts of Viṣvaksena. || 162 ||
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons who were experts in battle:
Cārudeṣṇa, a hero in combat.
And Pradyumna of great strength. || 17 ||
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, as well as Śarabha,
Cāru, and Cārubhadra.
Likewise, others [are] Bhadracāru and so forth. || 17 ||
Sucāru, Bhadracāru, Sudeṣṇa, Bhadra,
Paraśu, and Cārugupta.
And Cārubhadra and Cāruka. || 18 ||
Cāruhāsa and Kaniṣṭha were born, as well as the daughter Cārumatī; these were the offspring of Satyabhāmā.
Bhānu, Bhīmaratha, Kṣaṇa, Rohita, Dīptimat, Tāmrabandha, and Jalaṃdhama;
And four younger sisters were born to them. || 19 ||
To Jāmbavatī was born a son, Sāmba, who graced the assembly;
and to Rukmiṇī was born Cāruvidya.
And likewise Kanyā Cārumatī; Sānu, Bhānu, Akṣa, Rohita, and Mantravid. || 18 ||
Jarāndhaka, Tāmravakṣas, Bhaumari, and Jaraṃḍhara—
four were born among them.
The sisters [were born] from the one whose banner is Garuḍa. || 19 ||
Bhānu, Saubharikā, Tāmraparṇī, and Jaraṇḍhamā—
these are the daughters of Satyabhāmā.
Hear now of the offspring of Jāmbavatī: || 19 ||
Bhadra, Bhadragupta,
and likewise Bhadravinda,
as well as the renowned Bhadrabāhu.
as well as the maiden Bhadrāvatī. || 19 ||
Mitravān, Mitravinda, and the beautiful woman Mitravindā.
Mitrabāhu and Sunītha were the offspring of Nāgnajitī here;
understand that there were thousands of sons beginning with these. || 21 ||
That wise one had one hundred times a hundred thousand sons,
and eighty thousand more.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, one hundred thousand sons of Vāsudeva have been proclaimed. || 22 ||
Bṛhatī, Purubhāryā, Sītā, Sumadhyā, and Sugati were the daughters of the high-souled Bṛhaduktha, the descendant of Śini. || 22 ||
Her sons were three famous ones who graced the assembly:
the Aṅgadas, the Kumudas, and the Śvetas; and likewise there was a daughter, Śvetā.
Avagāha, Citra, Śūra, Citraratha, his son Citrasena, and likewise his daughter Citravatī;
and both Tumba and Tumbabāṇa, as well as Janastamba. || 22 ||
Upāsaṅga and Suta were his two sons, as were Vajrāru and Kṣipra;
Bhūrīndrasena and Bhūri were both the sons of Gaveṣaṇa. || 23 ||
The heir of Pradyumna was Aniruddha, the most intelligent of men, who remained unobstructed in battle by the daughter of Vidarbha.
From him was born Mṛgaketana. || 24 ||
Viṣṇu is established as their authority and their sovereign;
all the Yādavas are said to abide by his command. || 30 ||
Thus has the progeny of the Vṛṣṇis been recounted, both in summary and in detail;
it is worthy of praise and brings about the desired perfection of fame. || 30 ||
He who listens to this excellent [account] of the wise Kṛṣṇavaṃśa Sucaritra—
which bestows heaven and liberation and destroys great sins—
shall obtain a son if he is childless, and he who seeks wealth shall attain wealth. || 30 ||

## Section 4. The Genealogical History | Chapter 5 | B. (Bd. II. 71.1–195; H. 2136–2198; Mt. 47.30–168; P.1 I. 13.167b–267; P.2 V. 13.171–272a; Vā. 97.1–203; cf. A. 276.9–25) Learn now of the gods who possess human natures as they are being proclaimed: Samkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Sāmba.
And Aniruddha—these five are proclaimed as the heroes of the lineage. || 1 ||
The seven seers, Kubera, the Yakṣa Maṇivara, Śālaki, Nārada, and the learned Dhanvantari; || 1 ||
And Mahādeva with Nandin, as well as Śālaṅkāyana, and likewise Viṣṇu the Ādideva, together with these deities. || 2 ||
The sages said:
For what purpose was Viṣṇu born? How many past incarnations are remembered?
And how many other future manifestations will there be for that Great Soul? || 3 ||
Why is he born here in these peaceful fields of Brahmā? Tell us who ask you: for what purpose is Viṣṇu born again and again among men in the Vṛṣṇi and Ādhaka clans? || 4 ||
We wish to hear in detail and correctly all the deeds of the wise Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of his enemies; please speak! || 5 ||
O dear one, you ought to tell us the sequence of the Lord's actions, how his manifestations appear, and what his essential nature is! || 6 ||
How did that Blessed Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the enemies and desires of the gods, become the wise Vāsudeva within the lineage of Vasudeva? || 7 ||
Having abandoned the holy world of the gods, which is surrounded by immortals and adorned by those who have performed meritorious deeds, why have you come here to the world of mortals? || 8 ||
Hari, the leader of gods and men, the progenitor of the earth and the intermediate space—why did he enter his divine self into human form? || 9 ||
How did he, the best among wheel-bearers, while still a human being, conceive the idea of turning the mind-made wheel alone among men? (10)
How did Viṣṇu, the Lord who protects the entire world, become a cowherd and assume the state of a protector of cattle when he had gone to the earth? || 11 ||
How could he, the soul of all beings who supported and created the great elements, whose very womb is glory—how could he be held in the womb of a woman who wanders upon the earth? || 12 ||

By whom, having conquered the three worlds with three strides according to the will of the Thirty-three, the three paths of the world originating from the three aims of life were established. || 13 ||

He who, at the time of the end, having drunk up the world and made his body consisting of water, turned the universe into a single ocean by means of a path that is both visible and invisible. || 14 ||
He who is the ancient soul within the Purāṇas, assuming the form of a boar, the destroyer of enemies, lifted up the earth with the tip of his tusk. || 15 ||
He who, in former times, having conquered the earth, gave this imperishable triple world to the gods for the sake of Indra, that best of deities; || 16 ||
By whom, having assumed a lion-like body and then dividing that body into two parts, the former Daitya of great prowess, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was slain. || 17 ||
For he who was formerly the all-pervading Aurva and Saṃvartaka fire, dwelling in the netherworld and situated within the ocean, drank the oblation consisting of water. || 18 ||
They speak of that God who has a thousand feet, a thousand rays, and a thousand heads, appearing in thousands of ways throughout age after age. || 19 ||
That lotus, his ancestral home, which arose from the navel of the Ocean of Milk when the world had become a single expanse of water, was indeed free from mud. || 20 ||
By him those Daityas were slain in the Tārakāmaya battle, after he had made his body consist of all the gods and bear all weapons. || 21 ||
Mounted upon Garuḍa, he overthrew the arrogant Kālanemi;
he also conquered the great Daitya Tāraka and the mighty Asura Mahāsura. || 22 ||
In the northern region of the ocean, the Ocean of Milk, the ocean of nectar, he who lies down, having resorted to eternal yoga, [dispelling] the great darkness; || 23 ||
Surāraṇī conceived the divine embryo which Aditi bore in former times through the excellence of her asceticism;

he who, by the contempt shown toward the embryo, greatly distressed Śakra when he was besieged by the hosts of Daityas; and he who, having made the worlds his footprints, cast those Daityas down to dwell in the waters.
And having made the gods of the triple heaven his own, he appointed Puruhūta alone as the lord of the gods. || 25 ||
According to the rite of the Gārhapatya fire, by means of the Anvāhārya ritual, [he prepared] the Āhavanīya fire, the altar, the Kuśa grass, and the Sruva ladle. || 26 ||
He likewise performed the sprinkling, the boiling of the oblation, and the final purificatory bath;
thus, he established here the three offerings of sacrificial portions in the ritual.
He made the gods consumers of the *havya* offerings and the ancestors consumers of the *kavya* offerings;
he who, through the ritual of sacrifice, is the sacrifice itself for the sake of enjoyment within the sacrificial act. || 28 ||
The sacrificial posts, the fuel, the dipping-spoon, the Soma, the filter, and the enclosing-sticks;
likewise, the materials fit for sacrifice and the fires fit for sacrifice. (29)

He who, in former times, by means of his supreme office as the Lord of Creatures, distributed the sacrificial fees among the members of the assembly and the sacrificers at the Aśvamedha, the highest of sacrifices; || 30 ||
Having fashioned the three worlds in due order according to the respective ages, he likewise created moments,
twinklings of the eye, kāṣṭhās, kalās, and the three divisions of time.
The muhūrtas, lunar days, months, fortnights, as well as years, seasons, and divisions of time—these constitute the threefold measure within the three [periods]. (32)
Longevity, fields of merit, accumulation [of wealth], the primary marks, excellence of form, intelligence, heroism, and the mastery of the scriptures. || 33 ||
The three social classes, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three fires, the three times, the three types of action, the three lower realms, and the three qualities. (34)
By whom, through infinite action, the worlds and the gods were created;
by him, whose self is the host of all beings, the multitudes of all creatures were created. || 35 ||
He who delights in the practice of yoga preceded by the mastery of the senses, who is the leader of those who come and go, and who is free from attachment in all various circumstances; || 36 ||
He who is the goal of those endowed with righteousness, the non-goal of those of evil deeds, the source of the four castes, and the protector of the fourfold sacrificial office. || 37 ||
He who knows the fourfold knowledge and takes refuge in the four stages of life;
he is the quarters of space, the sky, the earth, the waters, the wind, and fire. || 38 ||
He who is the light of the moon and sun, the lord of the ages, and the ender of the night; he who is heard of as the supreme deity, and who is heard of as the supreme darkness. || 39 ||
He whom they call beyond darkness, he who possesses the supreme Self, the deity who is the Sun and others, and the all-pervading Lord who is the destroyer of the Daityas. || 40 ||
He who is the Ender at the end of the eons, and he who is the Ender of the world’s ender;
he who is the bridge for those who are bridges for the world, and he who is the pure one among those whose deeds are pure. || 41 ||
He who is to be known by those who know the Vedas, he who is the Lord of those whose nature is power;
he who becomes Soma for the gentle ones, and who becomes Agni for those with the splendor of fire. || 42 ||
He was the mind of men, the asceticism of ascetics, the discipline of those who act with prudence, and the splendor even of the splendid. || 43 ||
He is the body of all bodies and the goal of all who possess a goal.
Wind originates from space, and fire has wind as its life-breath. || 44 ||
The gods have fire as their life-breath, and Madhusūdana is the life-breath of fire.
From essence (rasa) blood is produced, and from blood flesh is said to arise. || 45 ||
From flesh, however, fat is born; from fat, bone is said to arise;
from bone, marrow was produced; and from marrow, the production of semen occurs. || 46 ||
From semen the embryo was produced through action rooted in [bodily] fluids;
therein, water is the primary constituent, and that is called the lunar aggregate (saumyo rāśiḥ). || 47 ||
The fire produced by the heat of the embryo is called the second heap;
one should know that the semen has the nature of the moon (Soma), while the menstrual blood has the nature of fire (Pāvaka). || 48 ||
These two states follow the flavors; the moon and fire reside in their potency.
Semen arose from the *kha* and *pha* groups, and blood from the *pitta* group. || 49 ||
The heart is the seat of phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta) is established in the navel. The heart is in the middle of the body; it is remembered as the seat of the mind (manas). || 50 ||
In that space between the navel and the abdomen resides the god Hutāśana (Fire);
the mind is to be known as Prajāpati, and phlegm is conceived as Soma. || 51 ||
For bile is known as fire; thus the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
When the embryo has thus been set in motion and has grown, resembling a cloud... || 52 ||
The wind, having united with the Supreme Self, performs the act of entering;
residing within the body, it is further divided fivefold as it expands. || 53 ||
The prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—prāṇa is its supreme abode; as it increases, [the body] grows. || 54 ||

The *apāna* [wind] is in the lower part of the body, the *udāna* in the upper part of the embodied being; the *vyāna* is that by which [the breath] is distributed throughout, and the *samāna* is in all the joints. || 55 ||
From that, his attainment of the elements arises as objects of the senses:
earth, air, space, water, and light as the fifth. || 56 ||
Established in all the sense organs, they each performed their respective functions.
They call the earthly element the body, and the vital breath the essence of life. || 57 ||
The apertures have space as their source; from water, the faculty of hearing proceeds;
light is the eye, whose essence is fire; and the mind is traditionally taught to be the controller of them all. || 58 ||
And villages as well as regions were set in motion by his power. Thus, the eternal Person, creating all these worlds, [proceeded]. (59)
"How did Viṣṇu come to attain human status in this world of mortals?
O wise one, this is our doubt; this is indeed a great wonder! (60)
How did he, the goal of those who seek their goal, assume a human body?
We wish to hear, O Viṣṇu, his deeds as well, in due order. || 61 ||
"Viṣṇu is described by the gods and the Daityas as the supreme wonder;
O high-minded one, tell us the wondrous account of Viṣṇu’s birth! (62)
Let this wondrous narrative, which brings happiness, be told;
let the manifestation of the Great-Souled Viṣṇu—whose strength and heroism are renowned, and whose deeds are marvelous—be recounted here in its true essence. (63)
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim to you the manifestation of that Great-Souled One, how that Blessed Lord of great asceticism was born among human beings. || 63 ||
O King, listen; I shall proclaim the most secret of secrets regarding how Bhṛgu, due to the sin of killing a woman and by the curse of Bhṛgu, was born as a human being.
Having cast off his divine body, Viṣṇu is born here among human beings.
Sūta said:
During the conflicts between the gods and the asuras, the Lord Hari is born;
formerly, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu ruled over the three worlds. || 67 ||
The kingdom was ruled by Bali, and subsequently, throughout the three worlds, there was a supreme friendship between those gods and the asuras. || 68 ||
Ten complete ages passed while the world remained untroubled;
and both the gods and the asuras remained equally obedient to their commands. || 69 ||
Once Bala was bound, this most terrible conflict broke out;
it was a great and horrific destruction of both gods and asuras at that time. || 70 ||
Indeed, for the sake of their inheritance, many battles occurred;
in this Varāha [Kalpa], twelve [cycles] are recorded, ending with the period of Ṣaṇḍa and Marka. || 71 ||
Now listen briefly to their names as I intend to speak of them:
the first is Nara-siṃha, and the second is Vāmana. || 72 ||
The third was the Vārāha, the fourth was the Amṛtamanthana,
and the fifth battle was indeed the most terrible Tārakāmaya.
The sixth is indeed named Āḍīvaka, and the seventh is likewise Traipura;
the eighth among them is named Andhaka, and Dhvaja is recorded as the ninth. || 74 ||
Vārtra is the tenth, and after that Hālāhala is remembered;
the twelfth among them is remembered as Ghora, and another is Kolāhala. || 75 ||
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Narasiṃha;
Bali was bound by Vāmana when he performed the conquest of the three worlds. || 76 ||
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in single combat by the gods;
he who was of great strength and great courage, undefeated in battles, [was killed].
Furthermore, the ocean was split in two by the Boar with his tusk. || 77 ||
Prahlāda was defeated in battle by Indra during the churning for the nectar;
however, Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was constantly intent on slaying Indra. || 78 ||
Having attained immunity from death through Bhava, as well as through special weapons and other means, that Jambha— who had been slain by Indra himself through valor during the Tārakāmaya war—
was killed in the sixth [battle] by Viṣṇu, who was possessed by Śakra. || 79 ||
When the gods were unable to withstand the city along with its deities,
all the Dānavas in Tripura were slain by Tryambaka.
The Asuras and Piśācas, as well as the Daityas, Asuras,
and Dānavas in the battle with Andhaka, and the Rākṣasas in the conflict with Andhaka—
all these were slain on every side by gods, humans, and the Pitṛs. || 81 ||
Vṛtra, joined by the Dānavas, was slain in the terrible Halāhala [battle];
he was then brought down by Mahendra with Viṣṇu as his ally. || 82 ||
Though skilled in yoga and concealed by illusion, Vipracitti, along with his younger brother, was slain by Mahendra at the banner after he had entered the very sign of the banner. || 83 ||

Surrounded by all the gods, Vṛṣa, having conquered the Daityas and Dānavas together in their entirety at Kolāhala, and having defeated Śaṇḍa and Marka along with the deities at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice; 84.
These twelve battles between the gods and the asuras have indeed taken place; they brought about the destruction of both gods and asuras for the sake of the welfare of all creatures. || 85 ||
King Hiraṇyakaśipu shone for one hundred million (arbuda) years,
as well as seventy-two [million], and additionally hundreds of thousands and millions (niyuta); specifically, seventy-two [millions] more.
And for eighty thousand years, he was the lord of the three worlds. || 86 ||
Furthermore, Bali was king for twenty-two million,
sixty thousand, and one hundred million years.
For as long as Bali held the authority of the kingdom,
for that same length of time Prahlāda remained withdrawn from the asuras. || 88 ||
O Indra, those three renowned and immensely powerful Asuras were said to have existed for ten yugas while this entire world remained under the dominion of the Daityas. || 89 ||
Consequently, this entire kingdom remained free from rivals for ten generations;
furthermore, these three worlds were protected without agitation by Mahendra.
For when this threefold world was taken from Prahlāda by the turn of time,
the sovereignty over the three worlds eventually came to belong to the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
Then, having abandoned the Asuras, the sacrifice approached the gods.
When the sacrifice had thus gone over to the gods, the sons of Diti spoke to Kāvya: || 92 ||
"While we looked on, our kingdom was seized; the sacrifice has been abandoned and gone to the gods.
We are indeed unable to remain here; let us enter the subterranean realm (rasātala). || 93 ||
Thus addressed, he spoke to them as they were despondent, consoling them with his voice:
"Do not fear; O heroes, I shall sustain you by my own splendor!"

Rain, the plants, the essences, and whatever wealth exists beyond—all these abide entirely within me; indeed, one quarter of them resides in the gods. All that I shall bestow upon you; I shall bestow it for your sake.
It was undertaken by me for your sake; all of that is now being maintained by me.
Then the gods, seeing them held captive by the wise Kāvya, consulted together, agitated by their desire for victory. || 96 ||
"This Kāvya is forcibly turning all of us away from this;
let us go quickly, before he can strengthen them further.
Having violently slain those who remain, we shall send them down to Pātāla. || 97 ||
Then the gods, becoming enraged, rushed at the Dānavas; being struck by them, O Jahnu, they fled toward Kāvya himself. || 98 ||
Then Kāvya, seeing those sons of Diti pursued by the gods, quickly protected them from the gods as they were terrified. || 99 ||
Having seen Kāvya standing there, the gods abandoned the Asuras without hesitation;
then Kāvya reflected.
Having reflected upon this beneficial word of Brahmā and recollecting what had occurred in the past, he then spoke to them: || 100 ||
The entire three worlds were conquered by Vāmana with his three strides;
Bali was bound, Jambha was slain, and Virocana was struck down. || 101 ||
The great asuras were slain by the gods in twelve battles; the majority of them, especially those who were foremost, were killed by various means. || 102 ||
"Since you are indeed few in number,
it is my opinion that there should be no further battle;
I shall devise a policy for your benefit."
"Wait for the turn of time;
I shall go to Mahādeva in order to obtain the mantra and achieve victory. || 103 ||
Then, having obtained from the god Maheśvara invincible mantras, we shall fight the gods again; thus you will surely attain victory! || 104 ||
Then those Asuras, having reached an agreement, said this to the gods:
"We have all laid down our weapons; we have all laid down our weapons. Without armor and without chariots, you indeed must traverse the worlds. || 105 ||
"We shall practice austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments. Having heard those words of Prahlāda, which were uttered with truth, [the sages agreed].
Then the gods turned back, free from fever and indeed delighted;
since the Daityas had laid down their weapons, they returned to their own abodes just as they had come. || 107 ||
Then Kāvya said to them: "Wait for some time;
remain free from anxiety and devoted to austerity, for time is the accomplisher of one's goals. || 108 ||
"O Dānavas, wait for me at my father's hermitage.
Having thus instructed the Asuras, Kāvya approached Mahādeva. || 109 ||
Having bowed down to him, the Lord who is the source of the world, he then said:
"O God, I desire those mantras which do not exist even with Bṛhaspati, for the defeat of the gods and the victory of the asuras. (110)
Thus addressed, the god said:
"O Bhārgava, perform these vows! O twice-born one, if you truly desire the mantras, then for a full thousand years, remain with your head downward, inhaling the smoke from a sacrificial pit."
If you drink it, may it be well with you; then you shall obtain the mantras. || 112 ||
Saying "So be it," Śukra, the joy of the Bhṛgus, having received the command,
touched the feet of the god and replied, "Certainly."
"O God, I shall perform the vow exactly as I have been instructed, O Lord!
Thereupon, appointed by the God, Kuṇḍadhāra became his smoke-producer. || 114 ||
Then, after Śukra had departed for the benefit of the Asuras,
he remained there in Maheśvara’s presence, observing the vow of celibacy for the sake of counsel. || 115 ||
Having understood that the kingdom had been abandoned by the Asuras according to political strategy,
the gods, led by Bṛhaspati and all grasping their weapons, then rushed toward them out of indignation at that vulnerability. || 116 ||
Seeing the hosts of gods with their weapons raised once more, all the asuras suddenly sprang up; terrified, they then said: || 117 ||
"The weapon has been laid down, safety granted, and the preceptor has entered upon his vow;
having bestowed fearlessness upon you, you have come against us with the intent to kill. || 118 ||
"O gods, we are without teachers and have abandoned the scriptures; we wear rags, bark, and skins, performing no rituals and possessing nothing. || 119 ||
We shall not be able to defeat even the gods in battle by any means whatsoever;
therefore, we shall seek refuge with the mother of Kāvya without fighting. || 120 ||
"We shall announce this distress until our preceptor returns;
and once Śukra has returned, we shall fight, clad in armor and bearing weapons. || 121 ||
Having spoken thus, they then, being terrified, sought refuge with one another and with the Mother of Kāvya;
she, for her part, granted them freedom from fear. || 122 ||
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! While you remain in my presence, it is not possible for fear to arise. || 123 ||
Seeing those Asuras thus supported by her, the gods then assailed them by force, without considering their relative strength. || 124 ||
Then, seeing those asuras being slain by the gods, the Goddess spoke angrily to the gods: "I shall bring about the state of there being no Indra! (125)
Having gathered all his equipment and quickly steadying himself through his impetuosity, he [challenged] Indra from the midst of the assembly. || 126 ||
The goddess, powerful, endowed with yoga, and rich in asceticism, made herself firm. || 126 ||
Then, seeing Śakra paralyzed, the gods fled like those who are bewildered, terrified upon seeing Śakra brought under control. || 127 ||
When the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra:
"Enter into me; may it be well with you; I shall carry you away, O Lord of the Gods! (128)
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu.
Seeing him protected by Viṣṇu, the Goddess became enraged and spoke these words: || 129 ||
"O Maghavan, I shall burn you along with Viṣṇu by my power, while all beings look on; behold the strength of my asceticism! || 130 ||
Overcome by her, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, became helpless.
"How may we both be released? Viṣṇu said to Indra. || 131 ||
Indra said: "Slay her, O All-pervading One, before she consumes us both!
I am especially overwhelmed; therefore, slay her without delay! (132)
Then, having observed her, Viṣṇu resolved to slay the woman; the Lord then meditated upon his discus, which immediately appeared before him. || 133 ||
Then he was filled with haste; as she was hurrying, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, acting swiftly and overcome with fear, perceived her— Viṣṇu then recognized that woman, the goddess.
The cruel intention of the Goddess; having perceived the cruel intention.
Enraged, he brandished that weapon and indeed severed the head out of fear;
seeing that terrible slaughter of a woman, the lord Bhṛgu became incensed. || 135 ||
Then Viṣṇu was cursed by Bhṛgu for the killing of his wife:
"Since you, though knowing the laws of righteousness, have slain a woman who should not be killed," || 136 ||
Therefore, you shall indeed be reborn among humans seven times;
for that reason, when dharma has been destroyed again and again by that curse, [you shall appear]. (137)
For the sake of the welfare of all in the world, he was born here among human beings. Having addressed Viṣṇu, he himself took that head.
Then, having brought water and taken it into his body, he said this:
"Truly, by means of Viṣṇu, I shall restore you to life. || 139 ||
If my entire dharma has been practiced, or even if it is known by me—by that truth, live on, if I am speaking the truth! || 140 ||
Then, having sprinkled her with cool water, he said, "Live!
As soon as his word of truth was uttered, the goddess was restored to life at that moment.
Then, seeing her as if just awakened from sleep, all beings heard the voices of the invisible ones resounding through the quarters, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent! (142).
When all beings were looking on, they saw that queen thus restored to life by Bhṛgu; it was like a miracle. || 143 ||
Seeing his wife restored to life once more by the unperturbed Bhṛgu, Śakra found no peace, for Kāvya had then performed a breach of his vow.
Then, while awake, Indra, the wise subduer of Pāka, reflected and spoke these words to his daughter Jayantī: || 145 ||
"For this Kāvya performs a harsh vow for the sake of one who is not Indra;
by him, O daughter, I have been made deeply agitated, even though he is wise. || 146 ||
Go, and attend upon him with auspicious means of dispelling fatigue, and with various services that are agreeable to his mind, remaining unwearied! (147)
"O daughter, propitiate that twice-born man in such a way that he may be satisfied.
Go; you have been given to him, so exert yourself for my sake! (147)
Having been addressed thus, Jayantī accepted her father’s words and went to where he stood, having commenced his formidable ascetic penance. || 147 ||
Seeing him drinking the smoke of the chaff with his face turned downward, and being struck down by the Yakṣa Kuṇḍadhāra, she [spoke] to Pāvana. (147)
And seeing that Kāvya was being cast down while the Goddess remained standing,
her own form pacified through meditative concentration.
One who is weak yet established in prosperity. || 148 ||
Then she, speaking so sweetly, praised her father with agreeable words and acted exactly according to the speech he had uttered in his poem.
Massaging his limbs at the proper time, she served him with pleasant touches; being attentive and compliant, she lived there for many years. || 150 ||
When that terrible smoke-vow was completed after a thousand years, Bhava, being pleased, then offered a boon to Kāvya. || 151 ||
This host has been overcome by you alone, and not by anyone else;
therefore, by your austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength— || 152 ||
And by your splendor, O Brahmin, you shall surpass all the gods;
whatever else belongs to me, O descendant of Bhṛgu, shall also be yours.

"The sacrificial Upaniṣads, along with their auxiliary branches and secret doctrines, shall all be revealed to you; however, this must not be spoken of to anyone. By means of that, you shall become a preeminent twice-born one who surpasses all. || 154 ||
Having thus granted boons to that descendant of Bhṛgu, Bhava further bestowed upon him the status of lord of progeny, the status of lord of wealth, and indeed invincibility. || 155 ||
Having obtained these boons, Kāvya’s hair stood on end with joy;
out of exultation, a divine hymn to Maheśvara manifested within him. || 156 ||
Then, standing sideways, he praised Nīlalohita in this way:
"Homage be to the blue-throated one, the foremost of the gods, the one of radiant splendor! (157)
Salutations to the one who causes the world to tremble, to the one who is to be licked, to Vatsara, O Lord of the World;
salutations to Kapardin, to the one with hair standing erect, to the one with tawny eyes, and to the giver of boons.
To him who is praised, who possesses excellent pathways, the god of gods, the impetuous one; to the one with the turban, the fair-faced one, the thousand-eyed one, the bountiful giver.
To Vasu-retas, to Rudra, to Tapas, to Cīravāsas, to Hrasva, to Muktakeśa, to Senānī, and to Rohita. || 160 ||
To the poet, the elder of kings, and the plaything of Takṣaka;
to the dweller on the mountain, the sun-eyed one, the ascetic, and the one who is ever-youthful. || 161 ||
To Suvṛtta, to Suhasta, to Dhanvin, and to Bhārgava;
to Sahasrabāhu and to Sahasrāmalacakṣus. || 162 ||
And to the one with a thousand bellies, to the one with a thousand feet, to the one with a thousand heads, to the creator of manifold forms. || 162 ||
To Bhava, to Viśvarūpa, to Śveta, and to Puruṣa; to the one who carries a quiver, to the one clad in armor, to the Subtle One, and to Kṣapaṇa. || 163 ||
To Tāmra, to Bhīma, to Ugra, and to Śiva;
to Mahādeva, to Śarva, and to Viśvarūpaśiva. || 164 ||
To Hiraṇya, Vasiṣṭha, Jyeṣṭha, and Madhyama;
to Babhru, Piśaṅga, Piṅgala, and Aruṇa. || 165 ||

To the wielder of the Pināka bow, to the one possessing arrows, to the variegated one, and to the ruddy one; to the one with the drum, to the one-legged one, to the worthy one, and likewise to the enlightened one. || 166 ||
To Śarva, the hunter of deer; to Sthāṇu, the terrifying one;
to the multiformed, the fierce, the three-eyed, and the Lord (Īśvara). || 167 ||
To Kapila, to the Sole Hero, to Death, and to Tryambaka;
to Vāstoṣpati, to Pināka, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva. || 168 ||

To the forest-dweller, to the householder, to the ascetic, and to the student; to the follower of Sāṃkhya, to the practitioner of Yoga, to the meditator, and to the one who has been initiated. || 169 ||
To Śarva, who is hidden, who is ascetic, and likewise all-pervading;
to him who is awakened, pure, liberated, and absolute.
To the one who is observant of the banks, to the great seer most devoted to sacred knowledge, to the four-footed, to the pure, to the armored, and to the swift-moving one. (171)
To Śikhaṇḍin, to Kapālin, to the fanged one, to the one who consumes the universe, to the incomprehensible, to the radiant, to Bhāskara, and to the wise Sumedhas. || 172 ||
To the cruel, to the deformed, to the loathsome, and to Śiva; to the gentle, to the meritorious, to the righteous, and to the auspicious. || 173 ||
To the one who is invincible, the immortal, the eternal, and the perpetual;
to the one with a tiger-skin garment, the Śarabha-like, the trident-bearer, and the three-eyed.
To the drinker of Soma, the drinker of clarified butter, the drinker of smoke, and the drinker of heat;
to the pure one, to the one who provides clothing, to the newly born, and to Death. || 175 ||
To Śarva, the eater of flesh; to Megha and Vaidyuta;
to Vyāśrita, Śraviṣṭha, Bharita, and Tarakṣu. || 176 ||
To Kṣema, Sahamāna, Satya, and Tapana;
to Tripuraghna, Dīpta, Cakra, and Romaśa. || 177 ||
To Pulastya, who possesses sharp weapons, who is pure, and who is perfected;
and to Rocamāna, Caṇḍa, Sphīta, and Ṛṣabha. || 178 ||

To the one who observes vows, to the one who is engaged in yoga, to the pure one, and to the one whose vital energy is directed upwards; to the destroyer of evil, the destroyer of sacrifice-obstructors, the slayer of death, and the one worthy of sacrifice. || 179 ||
To Kṛśānu, to Pracetas, to Vahni, and to Nirmala;
to Sikatya, to Prasanna, to Vareṇya, and to Cakṣus. || 180 ||
To Kṣipragava, Sudhanvan, Pramadhya, Piva, Rakṣoghna, Paśughna, Avighna, and Śvasita. || 180 ||
To the one who is bewildered, the great, and exceedingly difficult to traverse; to the skillful, the lowliest, and the Lord of the worlds. 181.
To the one who is free from disease, to the one who is vigorous, to the one established in equanimity, to the golden-armed one, to the truthful one, and to the one who brings peace. || 182 ||
To the one who is beyond conceptualization, to Māgha, to Hiraṇya, to the single-eyed one, to the most excellent, to Vāmadeva, and to the wise Īśāna. || 182 ||
To Mahākālpa, Dīpta, Rodana, and Hasa;
to the one with the firm bow, the one clad in armor, the one who possesses a chariot, and the one who possesses a protective fender.

To the Lord of the Bhṛgus, to Śukra, to the most eminent among the planets, to the wise one, to the unfailing one, to the profoundly peaceful one, and to him who is always dear to the Brahmins! || 184 ||

Homage be to you, O Blessed One, who are clothed in the quarters of space, who are clad in the skin, the universal one, the wearer of the tiger-skin! Homage be to you, the slayer of Bhaga! And homage to the Lord of Animals and to the Lord of Beings! || 185 ||
Salutation to you, the essence of mantra, who are the Praṇava, the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, who are Svāhā and Sudhā, and who are the supreme Vaṣaṭkāra! || 186 ||
Salutations to You, the creator, the sustainer, the fashioner, and the destroyer; to the Lord of the past, the future, and the present; salutations to You, whose very self is action! || 187 ||
Salutation to you, the divine self, who are indeed Vāsava, Sādhya, Rudra, Āditya, Aśvin, Viśva, and Marut! || 188 ||

Salutations to you, the soul of sacrifice, who know the ritual of Agni and Soma, who possess the sacrificial animals, mantras, and medicinal herbs, and who are the very embodiment of the sacrificial fee and the purificatory bath! || 189 ||
To the Lord of the self, to the one who has mastery over the self,
and to the one who surpasses all lords.
And for austerity, and for truth, and for renunciation, and for tranquility,
and also for non-violence and for non-greed.
And for one who is well-dressed and preeminent. || 190 ||
Salutations to you, who have become the self of all beings, the soul of yoga! Salutations to the earth, to the intermediate space, to the heavens, and to the Great One! 191.
Salutation to you, the soul of the worlds, who are Janastapā and Satya;
salutation to the Unmanifest, to the Great One, and indeed to the Element and the Sense-faculty! 192.

Salutations to you, the Great One (Mahat), who consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and is the essence of reality; salutations to the eternal, the signless, the subtle, and the conscious! || 193 ||
Salutations to you, the pure, the all-pervading power, the eternal self!
Homage to you in the three worlds—Svar, Bhuvar, and Bhūḥ! 194.
Obeisance be to You, the Truth, the End, the Great One, and the Four!
O Lord, whatever improper words have been uttered by me in this hymn of obeisance, You ought to forgive it all, for I am Your devotee, O Friend of Brahmanas! || 195 ||
## Section 4. Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 5. C.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, the Ruler Nīlalohita, he, bowing low and prostrating himself deeply, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: || 1 ||
Having touched Kāvya’s body with his hand, Bhava, filled with joy, granted him a full vision and vanished right there. || 2 ||
Then, when that god and his retinue had vanished, he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words to Jayantī: || 3 ||
Whose are you, O blessed one? Or who are you that are distressed when I am distressed?
For what purpose do you wish to conquer me, who am endowed with great ascetic power? (4)
O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion, I am constantly pleased by this devotion, humility, self-restraint, and affection! (5)
"What do you desire, O lady of noble form? What wish of yours may be fulfilled?
I shall fulfill it for you today, even if it should be very difficult to attain. (6)
Thus addressed, she said to him: "O most excellent of Brahmins, you ought to know through your ascetic power what I intend to do; for you truly know it as it really is. (7)
Thus addressed, having seen her with his divine eye, he said to her:
"O lady of beautiful hips, you are the daughter of Mahendra; you have come here for my benefit!"
"O lady of beautiful hips, O passionate one, you desire to enjoy union with me here for ten years, remaining invisible to all beings. || 9 ||
"O Goddess, dark as a blue lotus; O Goddess, with the luster of sapphire, worthy of the best boons, with beautiful eyes; O lady of lovely hips, with fair eyes;
choose this desire from me, O sweet-spoken one! (10)
"So be it; let us go home, O Mattakāśinī!
Then, having returned to his own home, the Lord was joined by Jayantī. || 11 ||
The descendant of Bhṛgu lived with that goddess for ten years, concealed by his illusory power (māyā) so as to remain invisible to all beings. || 12 ||
Knowing that Kāvya had arrived having accomplished his purpose, all the sons of Diti, joyful and desirous of seeing him, went to his house. || 13 ||
When they had gone and did not see the Guru, who was concealed by his power of illusion, they understood his characteristic and returned the way they had come. || 14 ||
But Bṛhaspati, having learned that Kāvya was restrained by the boon for the sake of his father, remained there for ten years out of a desire for the welfare of Jayantī.
Then, having perceived that opportunity and urged by Indra, he assumed the form of Kāvya and addressed the Asuras: || 16 ||
Then, seeing that they had assembled, Bṛhaspati said to them: "Welcome! I have arrived for the benefit of those for whom I am the officiating priest."
"I shall teach you, for that knowledge has indeed been attained by me.
Then, with joyful minds, they approached him for the sake of learning. || 18 ||
When those ten years were completed at that time,
Pūru’s intellect was suddenly born;
and at the end of that period, Devayānī’s intellect was likewise suddenly born.
Then he also set his mind upon supervising the patrons of the sacrifice. || 19 ||
Śukra said:
O Goddess of pure smiles, O virtuous lady with wide eyes of three colors and wandering glances, I am going to see those for whom you perform sacrifices. (20)
Thus addressed, the goddess said: "O observer of great vows, favor your devotees!
O Brahmin, this is the duty of the virtuous; I do not cause you to transgress your dharma! (21)
Then, having gone there and seen that the asuras had been deceived by the wise preceptor of the gods in the form of Kāvya, he spoke these words once again: || 22 ||
"O Kāvyas, grant me leave; for this is the sage Āṅgirasa.
Alas, O Dānavas, you have been deceived while I was occupied with him! (23)
Hearing him speak thus, the sons of Diti were then bewildered;
standing there with pure smiles, they gazed upon those two as they remained, one seated and the other standing. || 24 ||
All remained utterly bewildered and attained nothing at all;
then, while they were thus confounded, Kāvya spoke to them again: || 25 ||
"For I am your teacher, Kāvya; this Aṅgiras is the teacher of the gods.
Follow me all of you; abandon this Bṛhaspati! || 26 ||
When this had been said, all those asuras gazed intently at both of them, yet they could not discern any distinction between the two.
Bṛhaspati said to them: "This Aṅgiras is not agitated;
I am Kāvya, your preceptor, O Daityas, and this Bṛhaspati is merely my form."
"O Asuras, this one deludes you with my form!
Having heard his words, they indeed consulted together and then spoke these words: || 29 ||
"This lord has indeed ruled us constantly for ten years;
he is truly our guru. This twice-born man seeks some weakness within him. || 30 ||
Then all those Dānavas, bowing down and saluting him, accepted his words, having been deluded by long-standing association. || 31 ||
All the Asuras, enraged with blood-red eyes, said to him:
"This teacher is beneficial to us; go away, you are not our teacher! (32)
Whether he be Bhārgava or Āṅgirasa, this Blessed One is our preceptor;
we abide by his command—go now, please, without delay! || 33 ||
When all the Asuras had spoken thus, they sought refuge with Bṛhaspati.
When they did not comply, he spoke those words which were for their great benefit. || 34 ||
Then Bhārgava became enraged at their arrogance:
"Since you Dānavas do not resort to me, even though I have warned you. || 35 ||
"Therefore, having lost your senses, you shall surely meet with defeat!
Having spoken thus to them, Śukra then departed just as he had come. || 36 ||

Knowing that those Asuras had been cursed by Kāvya, Bṛhaspati, having achieved his purpose, was then delighted and resumed his own form; realizing the Asuras were now humiliated, he, having accomplished his aim, vanished from sight. || 37 ||
Then, when he had vanished, the Dānavas were bewildered and said to one another: "Alas! Woe! We have been deceived. || 38 ||
We have been turned away and struck from behind by the Creator; we have been burned by means of deceptive stratagems through his own illusory power regarding our respective duties. || 39 ||
Then the Asuras, terrified of the gods, departed in haste,
placing Prahlāda at their head and once again following Kāvya.
Then, having approached Kāvya, they stood around him with their faces cast down.
Seeing them returned once more, Kāvya spoke to those for whom he was the officiating priest: || 41 ||
"Since you did not rejoice in me when I awakened you at the proper time, you have therefore met with defeat because of that arrogance. || 42 ||
To Śukra, who was speaking thus with a voice choked with tears, Prahlāda then said: "O Bhārgava, do not abandon us—us who are your own patrons, who honor you, and especially your devotees. (43)
While you were not seen, we were deluded by that teacher of the gods;
you ought to protect us, your devotees, having perceived this with your far-reaching vision! || 44 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, if you do not show us favor, we shall enter the netherworld this very day, cursed by you. || 45 ||
Having understood the situation as it truly was, Śukra, out of compassion and pity, being thus entreated, then restrained his anger. || 46 ||
He said this: "Do not fear; you must not go to the netherworld (rasātala).
For this matter was destined to happen, and it has now come upon you while I am awake. || 47 ||
It cannot be made otherwise, for destiny is indeed more powerful;
the consciousness that has been lost by you today, you shall surely regain it. || 48 ||
"Having conquered the gods even once, you shall likewise enter Pātāla. 'The time for your turn has arrived,' thus spoke Brahmā; and by my grace, you have enjoyed the powerful three worlds. || 49 ||
Having ascended to the heads of the gods, he proclaimed his sovereignty for as long a time as ten complete ages (yugas) are called. || 50 ||
Furthermore, it is said that in the Sāvarṇika [Manvantara] your kingdom shall belong to you;
your grandson Bali will once again become the lord of the worlds. || 51 ||
Thus was this Kālā proclaimed by Brahmā himself as your grandson;
for when the worlds had been thus withdrawn, he truly found no further scope for his asceticism. || 52 ||
Since her activities were not motivated by desires, she was granted [this boon] by the pleased Aja during the Sāvarṇika interval. || 53 ||
"The kingdom of the gods shall belong to Bali," thus the Lord said to me;
therefore, he remains invisible to all beings, awaiting his time. || 54 ||
"Indeed, immortality was granted to you by the Self-born One out of affection;
therefore, being free from anxiety, do not suddenly become agitated over your turn. || 55 ||
"O Lord, I am not able to approach you;
I have been forbidden by Brahmā, who knows what is to come. || 56 ||
And these two disciples of mine are equal to Bṛhaspati;
they shall sustain all of you when you are embroiled with the gods. || 57 ||
Thus addressed by Kāvya of unwearied deeds,
the Daityas then departed together with those two, led by Prahlāda.
Having heard from Śukra that this matter was inevitable, the Dānavas,
placing their hope for victory solely in what had been spoken by Kāvya, [prepared for battle].
Then, all of them, armored and equipped with weapons, challenged the gods.
Seeing those asuras standing ready for battle, the gods [prepared themselves]. (60)
Then the gods, having donned their armor, fought them;
thus that battle between the gods and asuras continued for a hundred years.
The Asuras conquered the gods; defeated, the gods consulted together:
"We have been conquered by the Asuras through the power of Śaṇḍa and Marka. (62)
Therefore, with the sacrifice as our aim, we shall perform whatever is for our own benefit;
by means of this sacrifice, we shall summon those two [Rudra and Viṣṇu], and from that we shall conquer the Asuras. || 62 ||
Then the gods addressed both Śaṇḍa and Marka, and having summoned them to the sacrifice, they said to those two twice-born ones: "Abandon the Asuras! (63)
"We shall indeed seize you both after having conquered the Dānavas!
Thus did Śaṇḍa and Marka then abandon those Asuras.
Then the gods attained victory and the Dānavas met with defeat.
Abandoned by Śaṇḍa and Marka, the Asuras were overcome by the gods; for the Dānavas were thus rendered powerless. Then Śaṇḍa and Marka approached [the gods]. || 65 ||
Thus, in ancient times, the Daityas were then struck down by the curse of Kāvya. || 65 ||
Overcome by the curse of Kāvya and left without support, they were then bound by the gods and entered the netherworld (rasātala). || 66 ||
Thus were those Dānavas rendered devoid of effort by Śakra, from that time forward, through the curse and the agency of Bhṛgu. || 67 ||
When sacrifice had become lax, the Lord Viṣṇu was born again and again in order to establish the system of dharma and to bring about the destruction of adharma. || 68 ||
The Lord Brahmā declared that all those asuras who did not abide by the command of Prahlāda were to be slain by human beings.
From those dharmas, Nārāyaṇa was born during the Cākṣuṣa interval; then, during the Vaivasvata interval, Vainya set the sacrifices in motion. || 70 ||
At the manifestation of Vainya, Brahmā alone was the family priest. Then, when the fourth age had arrived and the gods had fallen into distress, (71)
Born within the ocean for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu, he became a second Narasiṃha; indeed, Rudra was his domestic priest. || 72 ||
In the worlds situated on Bali, during the Tretā age in the seventh yuga,
for the sake of Vāmana,
[it was performed] by means of Dharma with the priest as his guide.
Having contracted his body into his limbs before Bṛhaspati,
the delighter of Aditi’s lineage [Vāmana] [approached] the Daitya lord who was acting as the sacrificer.
Having become a twice-born, at an auspicious time, he spoke to Bali Vairocana:
"You are the king of the three worlds; everything is established in you. || 73 ||
"O King, you ought to grant me three strides," said the Lord.
"I grant them," King Bali, the son of Virocana, replied to him. || 73 ||
Recognizing him as Vāmana, he then joyfully gave [the land] himself;
O best of the twice-born, that Vāmana [then traversed] heaven, the atmosphere, and the earth.
