With three strides, the Lord traversed this entire world;
the Soul of Beings surpassed the sun with his own splendor. 73.
Illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions,
that one of great fame and mighty arms shone brightly, illuminating all the worlds.
Having seized the splendor of the Asuras and the three worlds, Janārdana brought the Asuras, along with their sons and grandsons, down to the depths of Pātāla. || 73 ||
Namuci, Śambara, and Prahrāda—these cruel ones were slain by Viṣṇu; cast out, they fled in all directions. || 73 ||
Mādhava manifested the great elements and the elemental self along with their specific qualities;
and there, O brahmins, he displayed a wondrous offering together with Vṛtra.
In his body he perceives the entire world as himself;
there is nothing in the worlds that is not pervaded by that Great-Souled One. || 73 ||
Indeed, upon seeing that form of Upendra, all the gods, dānavas, and humans were utterly bewildered, stupefied by the splendor of Viṣṇu. || 73 ||
Bali, along with his kinsmen and his circle of friends, was bound with great fetters;
the entire lineage of Virocana was settled in Pātāla.
Then, having bestowed the sovereignty over all the immortals upon the high-souled Indra,
the mighty-armed Janārdana appeared among human beings.
These three are known as his auspicious divine births;
now learn of his seven human births, which arose from curses. || 74 ||
In the Tretā age, however, Dattātreya was my tenth incarnation;
and when Dharma had perished, the fourth [incarnation] appeared, preceded by Mārkaṇḍeya. || 75 ||

at a time when Sūrya had been struck down by Svarbhānu and was falling from heaven to earth. || 8 ||
And when the world was overwhelmed by darkness, he by whom light was set in motion;
indeed, as the sun was falling, it was said to him: "May it be well with you! (8)
At the word of that brahmin seer, it did not fall from heaven to earth—he who, of great asceticism, established the most excellent lineages of the Atris. || 8 ||
He begot sons bearing the same names as himself upon those appointed daughters, he upon whom the wealth of Atri had been established by the gods during sacrifices.
Likewise, he had ten sons who were great beings devoted to fierce asceticism;
those brahmin sages, who had mastered the Vedas and established lineages, became renowned as the Svastyātreyas, though they were devoid of both Atri’s lineage and wealth. || 8 ||
O best of sages, listen as I shall fully declare the lineage of the son of Raudrāśva, the king; hear it, O twice-born ones. || 8 ||
The royal sage Anādhṛṣṭi had a son named Rceyu, and Rceyu’s wife was named Jvalanā, who was indeed the daughter of Takṣaka. || 9 ||
In that queen, that royal seer,
the lord of the earth Matināra,
begot sons who were the offspring of Matināra.
There are three who are supremely righteous: || 10 ||
Taṃsu was the first son, followed by Pratiratha and the righteous Subāhu;
and there was a famous daughter, Gaurī, the auspicious mother of Māndhātṛ.
All of them were knowers of the Vedas, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth;
all were skilled in weapons, powerful, and experts in warfare.
The son of Pratīratha was also King Kaṇva;
his son was Medhātithi, from whom the Kāṇvāyana twice-born ones descended. || 12 ||
O best of sages, she who was named Ilinī was indeed a woman superior [to all others],
a speaker of Brahman.
They approached him. || 12 ||
Then the son of Taṃsu was the royal seer Dharmanetra, powerful,
a proclaimer of the Veda, and valiant.
His wife was Upadānavī. || 13 ||
Upadānavī obtained four sons from Āīlin:
Duṣyanta, Suṣyanta, Pravīra, and Anagha.
The heir of Duṣyanta was the heroic Bharata;
he was known as Sarvadamana, possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, and was great. || 14 ||
A son was born to the high-souled Duṣyanta by Śakuntalā, namely Bharata, after whose name the Bhāratas are so called. || 15 ||
To King Duṣyanta, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father; he by whom one is begotten, he indeed is that [son]. (16)
"Support your son, Duṣyanta; do not disregard Śakuntalā!
O god among men, the sower of the seed rescues his son from the abode of Yama. (17)
"And you are the progenitor of this child; Śakuntalā has spoken the truth.
(This concerns Bharata, after the sons of the lord of the earth had perished.)"
But it was previously told by me due to the provocation of my mothers. (18)
Bharata, the son of Bṛhaspati Aṅgiras, was a wise and great sage who begot [sons] upon three women.
He begot nine sons,
yet the king did not rejoice in them, thinking, "They are not worthy of me. || 18 ||
Then those enraged mothers sent their sons to the abode of Yama;
thereafter, [the fate] of that lord of men...
That birth of a son was false. || 18 ||
Then that powerful Bharadvāja, the son of Bṛhaspati, was brought by the Maruts and restored to him by the Maruts through sacrificial rites. || 19 ||
In this very context, they cite this account of the wise Bharadvāja,
concerning the transmission of dharma to Bharata by the Maruts.
While his wife was pregnant, Uśija passed away;
then Bṛhaspati, seeing his brother's wife, spoke as follows: || 21 ||
"Adorn yourself well! O auspicious one, having adorned your own body, come to me for sexual union! Grant me sexual union, O auspicious one!
Being addressed thus, she said to him: "O Lord, I am indeed pregnant. || 22 ||
This embryo has matured and it utters the word "Brahman" with its voice;
you too have been one whose seed was never in vain, yet Dharma itself has been censured.
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati said to her with a smile:
"You must by no means instruct me in discipline! (24)
Rejoicing, he forcibly proceeded to have sexual intercourse with her;
then the embryo spoke to Bṛhaspati as he was rejoicing. || 25 ||
"For I was already established here previously, dear Bṛhaspati; moreover, you are one whose seed is never in vain, and there is no room for two [of us]. || 26 ||
Thus addressed by the embryo, he replied in anger: "Since, at such a time when all beings desire it... (27)

"You are forbidding me; therefore, you shall enter into long darkness! Then, having restrained his desire, he covered that [opening] with his two feet out of joy for Bṛhaspati. [The opening] of the mother was that of Bṛhaspati. || 20 || ... || 28 ||
That semen fell upon the ground; however, that semen, having been withdrawn between those two, became a child. He became a child who was not to be warded off.
Then, seeing that newborn boy, Mamatā said: || 29 ||
"I shall indeed go to my own home; support him, O Bṛhaspati!
Having spoken thus, she departed, and once she had gone, he too abandoned him. || 30 ||
Then, seeing the infant Bharadvāja abandoned by his parents, the Maruts took him up out of compassion. || 31 ||
At that time, Bharata, desiring a son, performed sacrifices in due order with many rites—both optional and occasional. || 32 ||
When that powerful sacrificer could not obtain a son, he then performed the Marutsoma sacrifice again for the sake of a son. || 33 ||
Thus gratified by that Marut-soma sacrifice,
those Maruts brought Bharadvāja to Bharata for the sake of a son—
a legitimate heir who was like a biological son to Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras. || 34 ||
Bharadvāja was transferred by the Maruts to Bharata;
and having obtained Bharadvāja as his son, Bharata then spoke to him:
"O Lord, once the progeny has been withdrawn, I shall have achieved my purpose through you. || 35 ||
The powerful Bharadvāja performed sacrifices with great rituals;
yet previously, when the birth of his son had indeed been rendered futile, he acted.
Then, from Bharadvāja, a son named Vitatha was born. || 36 ||
Therefore, from that Bharadvāja as well, there arose on earth Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas known by the name Dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas, who indeed had two fathers. || 36 ||
Then, when Vitatha had been born, Bharata went to heaven;
having consecrated Vitatha, Bharadvāja went to heaven, and the sage Bharadvāja departed for the forest. || 37 || Having consecrated his son, the ṛṣi [departed]. || 37 ||
And he, though himself false to his vows, begot five sons:
Suhotra, Suhotṛ, Gaya, Garga, and likewise the high-souled Kapila; these were the two sons of Suhotra. || 37 ||
And Kāśika was a mahāsattva, as was King Gṛtsamati;
likewise, from Gṛtsamati were born the sons belonging to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes. || 37 ||
Bhumanyu, however, was the heir of Vitatha;
Bhumanyu had four sons who were like the great elements (mahābhūta). || 38 ||
Bṛhatkṣatra was of great heroism, as was the powerful Nara and Garga.
Saṃkṛti was the son of Nara, and his two sons were possessed of great luster: || 39 ||

Gurudhī and Rantideva—both of these are remembered as the sons of Sāṃkṛti. And from Garga was born the learned Śini as his heir; from him the Śainyas and the Gargas are recorded as twice-born Kṣatriyas. || 40 ||
And Mahāvīrya’s son was the wise Urukṣaya;
his wife Viśālā indeed gave birth to three sons: || 41 ||

The highly illustrious [Trayyāruṇi], Puṣkarīṇa, and Kapi—these are remembered as the Urukṣayas, all of whom attained the status of Brahmins. These three great seers are declared to be the foremost among the Kṣatriyas descended from Kapi. || 42 ||
The Gārgas, Sāṃkṛtis, and Kāpyas—these twice-born ones were endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas—and the territory of Bṛhatkṣatra took refuge in the faction of Aṅgiras. || 43 ||
The heir of Bṛhatkṣatra was the righteous one named Suhotra;
the heir of Suhotra was indeed named Hastin, by whom this city of Hastināpura was formerly built. || 44 ||
"O best of the twice-born, hear now another lineage, that of Ājamīḍha:
Suhotra’s son was Bṛhat."
Bṛhata had three sons;
and Hastin also had three heirs who were supremely righteous.
Ājamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and the heroic Purumīḍha. || 45 ||
Ajamīḍha had three wives endowed with great fame:
Nīlinī, Keśinī, and the excellent woman Dhūminī. || 46 ||
At the conclusion of his great asceticism, virtuous sons who perpetuated the lineage were born to the aged and righteous King Ājamīḍha through those wives.
By the grace of Bharadvāja, listen to his detailed account!
From Ājamīḍha, through Keśinī, the powerful Jahnu was born. || 47 ||
It is said that from Ajamīḍha and Keśinī, the Kaṇvas were born. || 47 ||
His son was Medhātithi; from him the Kāṇvāyanas were born as twice-born brahmins. From Ajamīḍha, through Dhūminī, was born King Bṛhadiṣu. || 48 ||
Bṛhadanu’s son was Bṛhanta; Bṛhanta’s son was Bṛhanmanas;
and Bṛhanmanas’s son was known as Bṛhaddhanus.
Bṛhaddhanus was the father of Bṛhadiṣu, whose son was Jayadratha.
His son was Bṛhatkarman, and his son was Bṛhadratha. || 49 ||
Viśvajit was his son, and Senajit was his offspring;
now, Senajit had four sons who were world-renowned: || 50 ||
Rucirāśva, Kāvya, King Dṛḍharatha, and Vatsa, the king of Avanti—these were his younger brothers. || 51 ||
The heir of Rucirāśva was the highly illustrious Pṛthuṣeṇa;
the son of Pṛthuṣeṇa was Pāra, and from Pāra, Nīpa was subsequently born. || 52 ||
Nīpa had one hundred and eighty sons of immeasurable splendor;
all of them were known as the Nīpas and became kings. || 53 ||
The illustrious Samara, who increased the fame of the Nīpas and perpetuated their lineage, was born in Kāmpilya; he was one whose valor was truly desired. || 54 ||
Samarasya, Parapāra, and Sadaśva—these three sons of his were endowed with all virtues; among them, Pṛthu, the son of Pāra, shone forth. || 55 ||
From Pṛthu, however, was born by means of his well-performed deeds one named Sukṛta, who was endowed with all virtues; and Vibhrāja was his son. || 56 ||
The heir of Vibhrāja was the king named Aṇuha;
he was the son-in-law of Śuka, the husband of Kṛtvī, and possessed great fame. || 57 ||
The heir of Aṇuha was the lord of the earth Brahmadatta;
his son was Yogadatta, whose son was the highly illustrious Viṣvaksena. || 58 ||
Vibhrāja was born again here through his well-performed deeds;
he became Udaksena, the son of Viṣvaksena. || 59 ||
Bhallāṭa was his son, and Janamejaya was born from him;
for his sake, all the Niṣādas were destroyed by Ugrāyudha. || 60 ||
The sages said: Whose son was Ugrāyudha, and in which lineage is he celebrated? And for what reason were all those Niṣādas destroyed by him? || 61 ||
[Sūta said:
Ugrāyudha, a descendant of the Solar dynasty, performed austerities at Varāśrama for ten thousand years, remaining as motionless as a pillar; Janamejaya attended upon him. || 62 ||
Having promised him the kingdom, the lord struck down the two Nīpas;
he spoke various words of consolation, yet they indeed struck both of them as well. || 63 ||

To those who had come seeking refuge while being struck down, he said: "Because my word was not followed for the sake of protecting those who seek refuge, for that very reason I pronounce this curse upon you. (64)
"If I have performed ascetic penance, let it lead you all to Yama!
Then, as they were being dragged along by Yama before him, he [the sage]— 65 ||
Overcome by supreme compassion, he said to Janamejaya:
"You ought to protect these heroes who have departed from here for my sake! (66)
Janamejaya said:
"O you wicked ones of evil conduct, will you become his servants?
Having been told "So be it" by Yama, the king then fought for a long time.
Having forcibly conquered those [beings] along with Yama by means of terrible, hellish diseases, he gave them to the Sage; that was like a marvel. || 68 ||
Then Yama, being pleased, bestowed upon him the supreme knowledge of liberation;
having all performed what was appropriate, they departed for the imperishable Kṛṣṇa. || 69 ||
But those who adopt their conduct are not slain by untimely deaths;
they enjoy inexhaustible happiness both in this world and in the next.
The learned Yavīnara was born as the heir of Dvimīḍha.
Dhṛtimān was his son, and Satyadhṛti was his son.
Then there was the powerful Dṛḍhanemi, the son of Satyadhṛti;
and the sons of Dṛḍhanemi were the king named Sudharmā. || 72 ||
Sudharman had a powerful son, Sārvabhauma;
renowned as Sārvabhauma, he shone as the sole sovereign upon the earth. || 73 ||
In his great lineage was born the great delighter of the Pauravas;
and the son of Mahat was known as King Rukmaratha. || 74 ||
Now, the son of Rukmaratha was the king named Supārśva;
and the son of Supārśva was the righteous Sumati. || 75 ||
Sumati, too, was a righteous-souled, humble, and powerful king;
that humble monarch had a great son named Kṛta.
He was the disciple of the high-souled Hiraṇyanābha of Kauśala;
by him, the Sāma-veda collections were indeed proclaimed in twenty-four divisions.
They are remembered as the Prācyasāmans; the Sāmagas, however, are the composers of the Sāmans.
Then there was that hero Kārti, the son of Ugrāyudha and the delighter of the Pauravas. || 78 ||
There was one by whom, having displayed his prowess, the grandfather of Pṛṣata—the immensely energetic Nīpa, the lord of the Pañcālas—was slain. || 79 ||
The heir of Ugrāyudha was the highly illustrious Kṣemya;
from Kṣemya was born Suvirā, and from Suvirā came Nṛpaṃjaya;
from Nṛpaṃjaya was born Bahuratha—these are remembered as the Pauravas. || 80 ||
From Ajamīḍha and Nīlinī was born King Nīla;
through Nīla’s fierce asceticism, Suśānti was produced. || 81 ||
Purujāti was the son of Suśānti;
Bāhyāśva was the son of Purujāti; and there were five sons of Bāhyāśva.
They became like the immortals. || 82 ||
Mudgala, Śṛñjaya, King Bṛhadiṣu,
the valiant Yavīnara, and Kṛmīlāśva as the fifth—
these are renowned as being capable of protecting the five regions. || 83 ||
Because they were able to protect the five Pāñcālas, which were filled with prosperous districts, they became renowned as the "Pāñcālas. || 84 ||
The heir of Mudgala was the highly illustrious Maudgalya;
all these were great-souled beings.
The twice-born are endowed with the qualities of the Kṣatriya. || 85 ||
These Kaṇvas and Mudgalas have taken refuge in the faction of the Aṅgirases;
the eldest son of Mudgala was most devoted to sacred knowledge and possessed of great fame. || 86 ||
From Indrasena, Vadhryaśva was conceived;
from Vadhryaśva and Menakā, a pair of twins was born—so says the sacred tradition. || 87 ||
And the royal seer Divodāsa and the illustrious Ahalyā;
Ahalyā gave birth to the heir of Śaradvat. (88)
To that best of sages, Śatānanda, who was also possessed of great fame, there was a son named Satyadhṛti, who had reached the further shore of the science of archery. || 89 ||
Seeing an Apsaras before him, the seed of that Satyadhṛti was discharged into a clump of reeds, and from it a pair of twins was produced. || 90 ||
Śaṃtanu, who had gone out hunting, took it out of compassion;
because he remembered Kṛpa, she was called Gautamī, and likewise Kṛpī. || 91 ||
These are declared to be the Śāradvatas; these are remembered as the Gautamas.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the lineage of Divodāsa: || 92 ||
The heir of Divodāsa was the royal seer Mitrayu;
from him came Soma Maitrāyaṇa, and from him the Maitreyas are said to have descended. || 93 ||
These Bhārgavas, though endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas, have likewise taken sides [with the Pāṇḍavas]. The son of the high-souled Sṛñjaya was Pañcajana.
The son of Pañcajana was also Somadatta, a lord of the earth. || 94 ||
The heir of Somadatta was the highly illustrious Sahadeva,
and Sahadeva’s son was also...
There was a king named Somaka. || 95 ||
When his lineage had declined, Ajamīḍha was born again as Somaka;
Somaka’s son was Jantu, whose hundred sons shone forth. || 96 ||
The youngest among them was Pṛṣata, the powerful father of Drupada;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna was his son, and Dhṛṣṭaketu was his son. || 97 ||
These high-souled Somakas are remembered as the descendants of Ajamidha.
The great-souled Ajamidha had sons who bore the name Somaka. Now, Ajamidha’s queen was Dhuminī, who was longing for a son.
O best of sages, that highly fortunate lady was devoted to her husband, born of noble lineage, and she was intent on the practice of vows for the sake of obtaining a son. || 98 ||
Then, having performed most difficult austerities for ten thousand years,
she duly offered oblations into the fire.
He of great vows slept among the sacred kusha grass of the Agnihotra fire;
meanwhile, Ajamidha united with that queen Dhuminī. || 100 ||
He begot Ṛkṣa, who was smoke-colored and handsome.
From Ṛkṣa, Samvaraṇa was born; from Samvaraṇa, Kuru was born thereafter. || 101 ||
He who, having passed beyond Prayāga, established Kurukṣetra—which is meritorious, delightful, and frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds. || 102 ||
His lineage was very great, after whom the Kauravas were named. Kuru had four sons:
Sudhanvan and likewise Sudhanu. (103)
And Parīkṣit was mighty-armed, as were the excellent Arimejayas.
The heir of Sudhanvan is remembered as the wise Suhotra. || 104 ||
His son was Cyavana, a king skilled in dharma and artha. From Cyavana came Kṛtayajña, who, being a knower of dharma, performed sacrifices with various rites. || 105 ||
The king begot a world-renowned son named Vasu, a hero who was a friend of Indra, known as Uparicara Caidya, who could travel through the sky. || 106 ||
From Uparicara, the king of the Cedis, Girikā gave birth to seven sons who were men:
the great chariot-warrior Bṛhadratha, who was renowned as the king of Magadha. || 107 ||
Pratyagraha and Kuśa, whom they call Maṇivāhana;
Māruta and Yadu, Matsya, and Kālī as the seventh. || 108 ||
The heir of Bṛhadratha was the renowned Kuśāgra;
the learned and heroic son of Kuśāgra was named Ṛṣabha. || 109 ||
The heir of Ṛṣabha was the righteous one named Puṣpavān; his heir was the valiant King Satyahita, so it is remembered. || 110 ||
His son was Sudhanvan, and from him was born Ūrja;
Nabhas was the son of Ūrja, and from him that powerful one was born. || 111 ||
He was indeed born from two fragments, but he was joined together by Jarā;
because he was joined by Jarā, he is therefore known as Jarāsaṃdha. || 112 ||
This Jarāsaṃdha, possessed of great strength, was the conqueror of all kṣatriyas;
Sahadeva, however, was the powerful son of Jarāsaṃdha. || 113 ||
The illustrious Sahadeva’s son was Somādhi, who was possessed of great ascetic power;
Somādhi begot a son who was supremely righteous.
The lord who dwelt in Magadha was named Śrutaśarman. || 114 ||
The heir of Parīkṣit was the righteous Janamejaya,
as well as Śrutasena, Ugrasena,
and Bhīmasena by name.
All these highly fortunate ones are valiant and endowed with great strength. || 115 ||
Janamejaya had two sons, Suratha and the wise Matimat; and the son of Suratha was Vikrānta.
A son, Vidūratha, was born. || 116 ||
The heir of Vidūratha was the great chariot-warrior Ṛkṣa;
he became the second king.
He became famous by that very name. || 117 ||
O Brahmin, there are two Ṛkṣas in this Lunar dynasty,
and likewise two Parīkṣits;
there are three Bhīmasenas.
And there were also two Janamejayas. || 118 ||
Śrutaśravas, however, is proclaimed as the son of Somādhi, the king of Magadha. || 114 ||
The son of Janamejaya was the king named Suratha;
the heir of Suratha was—
Bhīmasena by name as well. || 115 ||
Jahnu, however, begot a son named Suratha, a protector of the earth;
and the heir of Suratha was—
King Vidūratha was a hero. || 116 ||
The sons of Vidūratha were also known as Sārvabhauma;
from Sārvabhauma came Jayatsena.
And his son was won over. || 117 ||
The Mahāsattva was propitiated; thereafter he was remembered as Ayutāyus,
and Ayutāyus was free from anger.
Therefore, he is remembered as Devātithi. || 118 ||
The heir of Devātithi was indeed Ṛkṣa; and of that second Ṛkṣa...
Bhīmasena was born as his son; from Bhīmasena came Pratīpa, and Śāṃtanu was the son of Pratīpa. || 119 ||
Devāpi and Bāhlika were indeed the three great chariot-warriors;
but Bhīṣma was born to Śāntanu.
In that lineage, O best of the twice-born. || 120 ||
Likewise, Bhīmasena was born from Ṛkṣa, and Dilīpa was his son. || 119 ||
Pratīpa was the son of Dilīpa,
and three sons are recorded for him: Devāpi, Śāṃtanu, and [Bhīṣma].
And Bāhlīka—these three are yours. || 120 ||
The heirs of Bāhlika were seven kings who ruled over Bāhlika;
and the son of Bāhlika was the highly illustrious Somadatta. || 121 ||
From Somadatta were born Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala;
Devāpi, however, departed for the forest out of a desire to pursue dharma, for the sage Devāpi became a preceptor of the gods. || 122 ||
Cyavana had a beloved son by that high-souled man;
meanwhile, Śāntanu became the king and the leader of the Kauravas. || 123 ||
I shall fully recount the lineage of Śāntanu, renowned throughout the three worlds;
and in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Mahābhiṣa:
Whomever he touches with his two hands, whether they be old or diseased, he becomes young again; therefore, they know him as Śāṃtanu. || 123 ||
Indeed, his quality of being a bringer of peace is celebrated here by all creatures.
Then King Śaṃtanu chose the daughter of Jahnu as his wife. || 123 ||
In her, that lord begot a son named Devavrata;
he was known as Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas. || 124 ||
Kālī gave birth to a son, Vicitravīrya, who was born as a slave; he was Śāntanu’s beloved son, a stainless soul whose very nature was righteousness. || 125 ||
And Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, in the field of Vicitravīrya,
begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however, begot one hundred sons upon Gāndhārī;
of them, Duryodhana was the eldest and the lord of them all. || 127 ||
Mādrī and Pṛthā were the two wives of King Pāṇḍu;
sons bestowed by the gods were born to them for the sake of Pāṇḍu. || 127 ||
From Dharma was born Yudhiṣṭhira; from Vāyu was born Vṛkodara;
from Indra was born Dhanañjaya, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra;
and Mādrī gave birth to Nakula and Sahadeva from the two Aśvins. || 127 ||
Five sons were born to Draupadī from the Pāṇḍavas;
Draupadī gave birth to Prativindhya as the eldest son from Yudhiṣṭhira. || 127 ||
Śrutasena was born from Bhīmasena, Śrutakīrti from Dhanañjaya, and the fourth, Śrutakarman, was born from Sahadeva. || 127 ||
And from Nakula came Śatānīka; these are proclaimed as the sons of Draupadī.
Beyond them, there are six other Pāṇḍava princes who are great chariot-warriors (mahāratha). || 1275 ||
From Bhīmasena, Hiḍimbā gave birth to a son, Ghaṭotkaca;
furthermore, from Bhīmasena, Kāśī gave birth to a son, Śarvagata. || 1276 ||
Mādrī gave birth to Suhotra from Vijaya; and Niramitra, the son of Nakula, was born of Kareṇumatī, the princess of Cedi. || 1277 ||
From Pārtha, Abhimanyu was born of Subhadrā;
and from Yudhiṣṭhira, Devaka was born as a son by Yaudheyī. || 1278 ||
Dhanañjaya was the son of Pāṇḍu,
and Saubhadra was his son; Parīkṣit, however, was the son of Abhimanyu.
He was indeed the father of Parīkṣit. || 128 ||
Parīkṣit, the conqueror of enemy cities, was the son of Abhimanyu;
Parīkṣit’s heir was...
Janamejaya was the king. || 128 ||
Two sons were born to Parīkṣit in Kāśī:
Candrāpīḍa, who became a king, and Sūryāpīḍa, who was a knower of liberation. || 1281 ||
Candrāpīḍa had a hundred sons who were supreme archers;
thus was the Kṣatriya lineage known on earth as Jānamejaya. || 1282 ||
Among them, the eldest was Satyakarṇa, the mighty-armed, who dwelt there in the city named Vāraṇasāhvaya; he was a performer of sacrifices who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
The powerful Śvetakarṇa was the heir of Satyakarṇa;
being childless, that righteous-souled one entered the forest of asceticism. || 1284 ||
Therefore, while in the forest, the daughter of Sucāru, the fair-browed Mālinī— whose very name implies a garland of crocodiles— conceived a child in her womb.
While he was still in the womb, Śvetakarṇa, the lord of subjects, followed the great and irreversible departure that had been undertaken previously. || 1286 ||
But having seen her beloved, that virtuous lotus-eyed daughter of Sucāru, Mālinī, followed after him into the forest. || 1287 ||
On the road, that young woman gave birth to a delicate little boy;
having abandoned him right there, she followed after the king. || 1288 ||
Like the virtuous and highly fortunate Draupadī of old, who was devoted to her husband;
that delicate prince wept upon the ridge of the mountain. || 1289 ||
For the sake of that high-souled one, clouds appeared;
and the two sons of Śraviṣṭhā, Paippalādi and Kauśika, [were present]. || 12810 ||
Seeing this, the two, filled with compassion, took them and washed them in water;
they rubbed his sides, which were drenched in blood, upon a stone. || 12811 ||
With his two flanks rubbed smooth and perfectly composed, he became dark like a goat;
indeed, those two flanks of his became as dark as a goat through the power of the god.
Then they gave him the name Ajapārśva;
he was raised by those two brahmins at Remakāśālā.
But Remaka’s wife bore him [the child] for the sake of a son;
he became the son of Remaka, while those two ministers were brahmins. || 12814 ||
Their sons and grandsons lived simultaneously for equal spans of life.
This is that very lineage of the Pauravas, the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
And on this subject, this verse was formerly sung by the wise Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, when he was delighted at the time of transferring his old age: 12816. [The verse follows]
"Without moon, stars, or planets, this earth might indeed become so; but it shall never at any time be without a descendant of Puru.
This renowned lineage of yours, the Paurava dynasty, has thus been described by me."
